trips.title: Clear Water, Thin Rescue: Kayak and Freedive the Albanian Riviera
trips.sub: Albanian Riviera & Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park
trips.summary: The Albanian Riviera has the clearest water on the Adriatic-Ionian arc and the least infrastructure to support you in it, and that combination is the entire character of this trip. You start at Vlorë for the one thing Albania protects properly, the Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park, reachable only by boat, with the Haxhi Ali sea cave, the ancient graffiti-covered quarry at Grama Bay and a Cold War military island you can only land on with a licensed operator. Then you cross the Llogara Pass and drop onto the Riviera itself: Dhërmi, Jala, the canyon beach at Gjipe, Himarë, Porto Palermo's castle on its own isthmus, and finally the Ksamil islets in the far south. Days are structured around a simple wind fact, the sea is glass until roughly one in the afternoon, when the maestral fills, so the kayaking and freediving happen in the morning. What you will not find is a lifeguard, a marked channel, a functioning recompression chamber nearby, or a phone bill you can predict. Plan for that and this is one of the most rewarding weeks of water in Europe.

trips.title: Maestral Country: Sailing and Sea-Kayaking Central Dalmatia
trips.sub: Central Dalmatia, Split, Brač, Hvar & the Pakleni Islands, Vis, Šolta
trips.summary: Central Dalmatia's afternoon is a machine. From roughly 11:00 the maestral fills from the northwest, builds through the early afternoon, holds 12-20 knots until about 17:00 and then switches off with the sun, which means every sailing leg, every kayak crossing and every windsurf session in this week has the same window and the same deadline. The trip is built around that: mornings on flat glass for kayaking, snorkelling and the Blue Cave, afternoons under sail or on a board. You move Split-Šolta-Vis-Hvar-Pakleni-Brač-Trogir, either on a bareboat if someone in the party holds a skipper's ticket and an SRC, or as a land-based version stitched together with car ferries and taxi boats. It suits competent, organised people who like a plan with a clock in it.

trips.title: Meltemi Weeks: Paros & Naxos on Board and Kite
trips.sub: Cyclades, Paros, Antiparos & Naxos
trips.summary: This is a week built around a wind that arrives on a timetable. From roughly mid-June the meltemi settles into the Cyclades as a northerly, filling in through the early afternoon and blowing itself out around sunset, and Paros and Naxos sit in the channel where it accelerates hardest. You base first on Paros, Chrisi Akti and New Golden Beach for windsurfing, Pounda for kite in the Antiparos channel, then take the 30-to-45-minute ferry to Naxos, where Mikri Vigla splits into a flat lagoon at Limanaki and a wave side at Orkos in the same ten-minute walk. The rhythm is the same every day: slow mornings, snorkelling and coffee, then a hard three-hour session from about 13:00. It suits an independent intermediate more than a first-timer, because in the second half of July the wind is often too strong for a beginner lesson to even run.

trips.title: The Bonifacio Funnel: Porto Pollo, La Maddalena and Gallura on the Wind
trips.sub: Northern Sardinia, Gallura, Porto Pollo & the La Maddalena Archipelago
trips.summary: Porto Pollo exists because of a geographical accident: eleven kilometres of open water between Sardinia and Corsica, and a northwest wind that has to squeeze through it. The Bocche di Bonifacio behaves like a venturi, and the maestrale that arrives at the sandy isthmus of the Isola dei Gabbiani has been accelerated on the way in. What makes the spot rather than merely windy is the isthmus itself, which splits the water into two entirely different sports within two hundred metres, a shallow, glassy lagoon on one side for learning and freestyle, an open bay with chop and a swell line on the other for wave riding and blasting. You spend the week on that isthmus, with three days out: one into the La Maddalena Archipelago National Park with its permit system and its no-go zones, one west to Capo Testa and the granite of Santa Teresa Gallura, one south to freedive the wall at Tavolara. The rhythm is fixed and generous, the maestrale is a genuine afternoon wind, so mornings are for coffee, boats and snorkelling, and from about one o'clock you sail.

trips.title: Fjord and Sandbar: Kayaking Boka Kotorska, Kiting Ada Bojana
trips.sub: Boka Kotorska (Bay of Kotor), the Ulcinj coast & Lake Skadar
trips.summary: Montenegro gives you two completely different pieces of water in one small country, and this week takes both. The first half is the Boka Kotorska, a drowned river canyon that looks like a fjord and behaves like a lake, glassy at dawn, framed by 1,700 m limestone walls, with Perast's two islets, the church above Stoliv and half a dozen abandoned villages you can only sensibly reach by kayak. The second half is the exact opposite: the Ulcinj coast, where 12 kilometres of open sand at Velika Plaža runs down to the Bojana river and the flat, shallow lagoon at Ada Bojana that has quietly become one of Europe's best beginner and freestyle kite spots. Between the two you get the Blue Cave and Žanjice at the bay's mouth, and you end on freshwater at Lake Skadar, the largest lake in the Balkans, paddling through lily fields under a national park. The wind story is simple and worth learning: the maestral is your friend and arrives after lunch, and the bura is the reason you check the forecast every single morning.

trips.title: Reserve and Peninsula: Surfing Ericeira, Peniche and the Nazaré Canyon
trips.sub: Estremadura, Ericeira World Surfing Reserve, Peniche & Nazaré
trips.summary: This is Portugal's densest stretch of good waves and it fits inside a 70 km drive. You start in Ericeira, the only World Surfing Reserve in Europe, where seven or eight genuinely world-class reefs sit inside four kilometres of coast and a beginner can still find a sand-bottomed beach break at Foz do Lizandro. Then you move to Peniche, which is not a town so much as a peninsula, and because it sticks out into the Atlantic with waves on both sides, it works in almost any wind, which is the single most useful geographical fact in Portuguese surfing. You finish north at Nazaré, where a 230 km submarine canyon focuses swell into Praia do Norte and where, in the right season, you stand on the fort headland and watch waves that do not look real. Two hard truths shape the week: the nortada, a thermal north wind that ruins the afternoon most days from spring to early autumn, and a 3.5 m spring tidal range that turns each break on and off. Learn both and this is one of the best surf weeks in Europe.

trips.title: Two Winds, One Town: Kiting Tarifa and the Costa de la Luz
trips.sub: Cádiz, Tarifa, the Strait of Gibraltar & the Costa de la Luz
trips.summary: Tarifa is not one destination but two, and which one you get is decided every morning by a single question: levante or poniente. The levante is the hot, gusty, sometimes savage easterly that pours out of the Mediterranean through the Strait and can hold 35 knots for four days running; the poniente is the cooler, smoother westerly off the Atlantic that comes in side-onshore and turns the same beaches into something a sane intermediate can enjoy. This week teaches you to read that difference and to move accordingly, Los Lances and Valdevaqueros on poniente, Balneario and Punta Paloma's wind shadow on levante, Bolonia when everything is too much and you want space. Between sessions you get things almost no other kite destination can offer: a Roman town with its forum still legible in the sand at Bolonia, pilot whales and orcas in the Strait, Atlantic beach breaks at El Palmar forty minutes north, and a one-hour ferry to Tangier. It suits an independent intermediate who is happy to drive, read a forecast, and change plan at 09:00.
